vignette: James, a 49-year-old plumber with North American ethnicity and married to his partner, has been grappling with severe PTSD following physical abuse by his romantic partner. The traumatic event, which occurred several months ago, left deep emotional scars that continue to affect James' daily life. The night of the trauma remains vivid in James’ mind. He recalls the intense argument escalating into a violent confrontation where he was physically abused. The smell of burnt food from the kitchen lingered in the air, becoming an olfactory danger cue tied to the traumatic experience. Since then, any faint whiff of burnt food sends waves of panic through him, triggering memories of that night. James has developed several maladaptive strategies as a response to these triggers. One of his primary coping mechanisms is staying up late into the night, often until very early hours. This behavior began shortly after the traumatic event when he found himself unable to sleep due to intrusive thoughts and nightmares. The burnt smell in particular causes him to lie awake, hyper-vigilant and anxious, as if waiting for another attack. James also avoids thinking about the event itself. Whenever memories of that night begin to resurface—especially during moments of quiet or solitude—he diverts his attention elsewhere. This avoidance becomes particularly pronounced when he encounters other triggers like confrontations or expressions of anger from others, even if they are calm and controlled. These situations often send him into a state of heightened anxiety, prompting him to withdraw mentally. His occupation as a plumber has not been immune to these changes. James finds himself avoiding certain job sites where the smell of burnt food might be present, especially in older homes with poorly maintained kitchens. This avoidance leads to significant stress and occasional missed work appointments, which strains his relationship with clients and colleagues who rely on him for timely services. James’ marriage has also been affected by these changes. He becomes irritable and distant whenever his partner expresses any form of anger or frustration, even if it is justified. His partner notices the tension and tries to be supportive, but James often isolates himself further, believing that he will somehow prevent another traumatic event by distancing himself from potential conflict. The burnt smell remains a potent trigger for James. Even brief exposures can cause him to feel overwhelmed with anxiety, leading him to stay up late, hyper-vigilant and restless. This pattern has become self-reinforcing; the more anxious he feels due to triggers, the later he stays awake, further exhausting his mental resources. What finally brought James to seek help was a recent incident where he nearly missed an important job appointment because of his avoidance behavior. The realization that his maladaptive strategies were beginning to disrupt his professional life and relationships pushed him to consider therapy. Despite feeling vulnerable, James is hopeful that with support, he can regain control over his thoughts and behaviors. James’ fears are centered around the possibility of another violent confrontation and the anxiety it brings. He hopes that through therapy, he can learn more effective coping mechanisms and reduce the impact these triggers have on his daily life. His current state reflects a deep desire to reclaim his peace of mind and rebuild the trust in his relationships.
